Operation Economic Outcast Targets Iran’s International Financial Networks and Shadow Banking Architecture
body: October 15, 2026 Action Disrupts Iraqi Bank Enabling Iranian Sanctions Evasion and Cuts Off Key Foreign Currency Lifelines WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury disrupted Iran’s efforts to infiltrate the international financial system through an Iraqi bank that also supports Iran’s terrorist proxy militia groups.  By dismantling these institutions—including offshore banks and shadow financiers that have moved hundreds of millions of dollars through shell companies and foreign‑exchange specialists across the Middle East and Asia—Treasury is severing critical revenue streams that sustain Iran’s military and proxy forces. “The noose is tightening around Iran’s economy, and not even Iran’s so-called allies can save it,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “The Department of the Treasury will not relent until the Iranian regime’s coffers are empty and every remaining financial lifeline sustaining its war machine has been severed.” In coordination with today’s action, the U.S. Department of State is concurrently designating Cuba-based Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of Executive Order (E.O.) 14404 for operating in or having operated in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy.  BICSA has provided services to the designated Iran-based Karafarin Bank since at least 2022. These designations, coupled with additional sanctions on Iran’s shadow banking networks, cut off some of the few remaining financial lifelines the regime can access to prop up its failing economy and fund its military.  The designations also expose the regime’s deliberate use of complex offshore structures and front companies to circumvent sanctions and stabilize its economy despite mounting pressure.  Taken together, today’s measures target the core financial architecture that enables Iran to evade international scrutiny and fund its destabilizing regional activities.  Treasury’s action is being taken pursuant to E.O. 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, including Iran’s financial and petroleum sectors. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026, dubbed Economic D-Day, Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime. Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system.  It also expanded secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . Because Iran is already subject to comprehensive U.S. sanctions, it relies on multi-jurisdictional shadow banking networks to generate revenue and transfer funds abroad.  Iran uses these shadow banking networks to launder funds, procure weapons, access U.S. dollar correspondent banking relationships, and bankroll its regional terrorist proxy groups.  These networks rely on financial institutions such as the recently designated Golden Global Bank , and Operation Economic Outcast will continue to identify these banks and remove their access to the U.S. dollar. IRAQI BANK PROVIDING U.S. DOLLAR ACCESS FOR IRAN Iraq-based International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (IDB) provides financial facilitation services and U.S. dollar access for Iran.  IDB has abused its access to the now-dissolved U.S. dollar wire auction and maintains ties to Iranian government entities and Iran-aligned militia groups (IAMGs) in Iraq.  IDB was initially established by Iranian companies to support the Iranian economy and supply Iran with U.S. dollars.  U.S.-designated Bank Melli , which was located next to IDB in Iraq, closed due to U.S. sanctions and transferred its capital to IDB.  IDB uses Iranian capital to conduct business, then collects any profit made and sends it back to Iran in the form of U.S. dollars each month.  The bank’s current leadership received ownership of IDB from a dual-Iranian Iraqi financier working for the U.S.-designated Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps–Qods Force (IRGC-QF).  The financier continues to use his familial relationships to exert influence over the bank. IDB is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. IRANIAN “OFFSHORE” BANKS In addition to establishing correspondent banking relationships with financial institutions in allied countries, the Iranian government has authorized certain banks to operate “ offshore ” in free trade zones.  These Iranian banks have been approved by the Central Bank of Iran and the Supreme National Security Council to conduct their operations using foreign currency to aid sanctions evasion schemes.  Iran-based Jazireh International Bank Company is an Iranian offshore bank affiliated with Bank Mellat, while Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company is an offshore bank affiliated with Bank Shahr. Jazireh International Bank Company and Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. IRANIAN OIL “TRUSTEE” Many of Iran’s key revenue generation streams are corruptly controlled by Iranian regime elites.  These revenue streams include the shipping empire of Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani , son of Ali Shamkhani, the late advisor to Iran’s Supreme Leader, and the vast overseas property holdings of Ali Ansari , a key benefactor of Mojtaba Khamenei.  One of the elites controlling Iran’s key revenue streams is Iranian national Sayyed Ruhollah Razavi (Razavi), son-in-law of Iran’s hardline Paydari Front leader and one of the top oil trustees on whom the Iranian regime relies to sell oil and repatriate the revenue. Living in Dubai as one of Iran’s top oil intermediaries, Razavi has worked hand-in-hand with Seyed Naiemaei Badroddin Moosavi , a Hizballah financier and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force facilitator designated on April 15, 2026.  Prior to the U.S. blockade preventing Iranian oil exports, Razavi was responsible for shipping millions of barrels of oil overseas each month on behalf of the National Iranian Oil Company and its subsidiary, Naftiran Intertrade Company.  Razavi has also used his network to move the revenue generated from these oil sales through Iran’s clandestine banking system of shell companies and cash and gold couriers.  These networks move funds through Hong Kong to the UAE and Türkiye where they are converted to gold and cash and then smuggled on Mahan Air flights to Iran and its terrorist proxies around the world.  Razavi is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. In addition to his overseas work on behalf of Iran, Razavi manages Iran-based companies Tejarat Gostar Atlas Parsian Kish Company and Farzanegan Energy Pars Company , the latter of which is currently developing the Farzanegan Gas Condensate Refinery in Iran’s Bushehr Province.  Tejarat Gostar Atlas Parsian Kish Company and Farzanegan Energy Pars Company are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Razavi. SHADOW BANKING OPERATIVES Farab Sorough Qeshm Company (FSAQ), an affiliate of Iran’s Shahr Bank, relies on a cadre of foreign exchange experts to process transactions essential to the operations of Iran’s leading oil sales companies and brokers, including the National Iranian Oil Company, Triliance Petrochemical Company, and the military-controlled Sepehr Energy Jahan Nama Pars Company.  FSAQ employees help to coordinate financial transactions through its rahbar network using shell companies established in Hong Kong and the UAE.  Today, OFAC is designating seven FSAQ employees who have been involved in foreign exchange operations linked to FSAQ: Zhila Mohammadi , Milad Katebi , Amir Sabeti , Nazanin Borji , Fatemeh Vasighi Meraji , Azadeh Abdolalipur , and Farzad Allahyar .  Hong Kong-based Elitesphere Trading Co., Limited , which has been used by FSAQ to move funds through the rahbar network of brokers and front companies in support of Iranian sanctions evasion, is also being designated for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy. Zhila Mohammadi, Milad Katebi, Amir Sabeti, Nazanin Borji, Fatemeh Vasighi Meraji, Azadeh Abdolalipur, and Farzad Allahyar are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, FSAQ. Iran-based exchange house Seyyed Abbas Hosseini Parsa and Partners Qeshm General Partnership (Hosseini Parsa Exchange), owned and operated by Iranian nationals Seyyed Abbas Hosseini Parsa and Khaled Mohiesnejad , assists the rahbar financial activities of sanctioned Iranian banks alongside Dominican/Iranian national Sadegh Bavi .  Sadegh Bavi, an IRGC-Qods Force facilitator and money launderer who also assists in weapons purchases for Iran, is the owner and general manager of the Bavi General Trading Company LLC , which was previously designated by OFAC for helping coordinate tens of millions of dollars’ worth of payments for front companies operated by the Persian Gulf Petrochemical Industry Commercial Co. and Triliance Petrochemical Co. Ltd .  Hosseini Parsa Exchange has a close relationship with Bavi General Trading, which has used Hosseini Parsa Exchange’s official documents and letterhead to carry out its own business operations.  Sadegh Bavi also owns and operates Bavi and Partners Exchange Company , another Iran-based currency exchange house. Iran-based exchange house Soheil and Sorush Najafzadeh and Partners Company (Najafzadeh Exchange), owned and operated by Iranian nationals Sorush Najafzadeh , Soheil Najafzadeh , and Mansureh Mirmohammadi , has processed transactions worth hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of financial transactions for Iranian financial institutions, including entities linked to Bank Mellat and its rahbar, Tejarat Sarir Afrooz Kish .  Iran-based exchange house Abolhasan Jalali and Partners Exchange Company (Jalali Exchange), owned and operated by Iranian nationals Abolhassan Jalali and Ensiyeh Mullah Mohammadi , has likewise facilitated tens of millions of dollars’ worth of payments for Iran’s shadow banking networks and sanctioned rahbar entities. Elitesphere Trading Co., Limited, Hosseini Parsa Exchange, Jalali Exchange, Najafzadeh Exchange, Bavi and Partners Exchange Company, Sorush Najafzadeh, Soheil Najafzadeh, Abolhassan Jalali, Ensiyeh Mullah Mohammadi, and Sadegh Bavi are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy.  Seyyed Abbas Hosseini Parsa and Khaled Mohiesnejad are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Hosseini Parsa Exchange.  Mansureh Mirmohammadi is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Najafzadeh Exchange. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons. OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing or conspiring to cause U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, and from engaging in conduct that evades U.S.  sanctions. Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.  In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons. Furthermore, engaging in certain transactions involving the persons designated today may risk the imposition of secondary sanctions on participating foreign financial institutions.  OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List), but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior. For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on Filing a Petition for Removal from an OFAC List . Click here for more information on the persons designated today . ###

title: Statement from U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent for the World Bank Development Committee and IMF International Monetary and Financial Committee
body: October 14, 2026 This year’s Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank provide an important opportunity to engage on current global economic challenges as well as our work with partners and the international financial institutions to support a pro-growth agenda, macroeconomic and financial stability, and poverty reduction.  We thank Thailand for hosting us for the Annual Meetings. In the United States, President Trump’s America First Investment Policy is promoting robust economic growth and prosperity, fiscal prudence, energy abundance, and regulatory modernization.  Internationally, we are getting back to basics by forging a broad consensus on the need to promote growth as the key condition on which durable prosperity depends.  As G20 President, the United States is focused on promoting strong economic growth, and has prioritized increasing productivity, addressing global imbalances, engaging with the private sector, advancing financial literacy, improving the sovereign debt architecture, and promoting financial sector innovation and regulatory modernization.  When focused on their core missions, the IMF and World Bank are well-placed to help advance these important objectives. The IMF is making progress at getting back to basics.  Through recent policy reviews, the IMF is upgrading its policy toolkit for surveillance and lending and restoring its focus on its core responsibilities.  This includes the external sector issues at the heart of the IMF’s mandate, strengthening surveillance of debt vulnerabilities in low-income countries, and making the financial sector surveillance more risk-based.  Moreover, the IMF has rightly focused on strengthening program design to enhance the effectiveness of IMF-supported reform programs to durably address balance of payments challenges and restore external viability. One area where this refocus must go further is in the IMF’s work on global imbalances.  This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances.  Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment.  The IMF was founded to prevent these kinds of distortive policies and negative spillovers, and must exercise its voice on this critical issue or risk being sidelined. With recent major policy reviews complete, the hard work of implementation begins.  The United States will hold the IMF accountable for translating these reforms into stronger surveillance, more effective lending, and more robust assessment of debt sustainability.  Successfully delivering on the IMF’s core mandate will require commitment from IMF management to be an unflinching truth-teller through surveillance and to hold borrowers accountable in IMF-supported programs.  That same commitment is required of the authorities undertaking painful but necessary macroeconomic adjustments and structural reforms. The IMF must continue to prioritize its work and focus its resources on its core mandate.  New and emerging issues warrant IMF engagement only where they are clearly macrocritical and within the Fund’s mandate, and adding new priorities should require reducing lower-value work, rather than continually expanding the Fund’s agenda such as financing provided through the Resilience and Sustainability Trust that lacks a clear linkage to balance of payments pressures and veers into development-policy lending. The IMF has sufficient resources to accomplish its mission.  The United States remains committed to a strong, quota-based, and adequately resourced IMF, and we continue to work to secure congressional approval for the 16 th General Review of Quotas.  Future quota reviews should be based on resource adequacy needs, as reflected in the recently approved Diriyah Guiding Principles on IMF Quota and Governance Reforms.  Any future quota realignment should reflect members’ relative position in the world economy and be based on a new quota formula. After years of mission creep, the World Bank is beginning to refocus on its core mission of reducing poverty and raising economic growth.  Over the last year, the Bank has strengthened its development agenda by further implementing its jobs initiative, removing inefficient and distortionary climate finance targets, beginning to phase out lending to certain advanced client countries that have not needed Bank support for years, taking steps to better implement its graduation policy, and devising a strategy for supporting a more diversified minerals value chain. These are necessary steps in returning the Bank to its core mission, but significantly more is needed.  The Bank must promote country self-reliance by deploying resources where they are most needed and impactful, graduating more advanced countries from Bank support, delivering better access to reliable, affordable, and abundant energy, and increasing competition and quality in Bank-financed procurement to improve development outcomes.  And, in doing these things, the Bank must be more efficient and selective, pursuing operations with the greatest development impact, rather than simply pushing as much money as possible out the door. We expect the Bank to phase out sovereign lending to countries that have long since met the graduation policy criteria so that the Bank can refocus its resources where they are most needed and impactful.  Despite being long overdue, the planned phase outs of lending to China and Poland represent an important milestone for both countries.  As the Bank continues to implement the graduation policy, we expect to see Graduation Progress Notes that meaningfully assess where graduation-eligible countries fall short of meeting the graduation criteria, and associated Country Partnership Frameworks focusing Bank programming on addressing those shortcomings.  As the Bank enters the longest period in its history without a country graduating from lending eligibility, World Bank Management should take concrete steps to ensure that graduations resume. Similarly, the International Development Association (IDA) must facilitate graduation so that it can focus its resources on the poorest countries where its investments in foundational infrastructure, as well as in reforms that promote debt sustainability and transparency, enhanced domestic resource mobilization, and strong public financial management, help countries develop and stand up to coercive and opaque lending terms from some creditors.  As we discuss IDA’s resources over the next 15 months, IDA must clearly identify its accomplishments in boosting growth, and reducing poverty.  We also support extending the deadline for low-income countries to subscribe to the shares allocated under the 2018 capital increases, helping them preserve and strengthen their representation and voice in the institution. Contributing to country self-reliance also requires the Bank to focus more on the sectors most critical to development and industrialization, chief among them reliable and affordable energy.  Energy abundance sparks economic abundance.  We continue to support the World Bank and African Development Bank goal to extend energy access to 300 million more people in Africa.  Achieving this goal will require the Bank to take a technology-neutral approach rather than restricting borrower choice, including by removing constraints on its support for natural gas and positively responding to borrower demand for gas projects.  Accordingly, the World Bank Group should formally retire its prohibition on financing upstream gas and oil.  The Bank cannot credibly invoke country ownership while categorically excluding upstream projects before their development merits are even assessed. We welcome the recent approval of an IDA project to secure near-term gas supply, prepare mid-and downstream investments, and develop gas strategies in West Africa.  Ultimately, success must be measured by whether countries gain the energy access needed to drive growth, create jobs, and reduce poverty.  We therefore welcome the move to focus on outcomes rather than on arbitrary targets.  To further support energy abundance, the United States is also making an initial contribution to the Nuclear Energy Assistance Trust Fund, which will help countries lay the groundwork for future nuclear energy investments. Critical minerals are foundational inputs to growth and economic security.  We welcome the Bank’s recently approved Metals and Minerals Implementation Plan.  The Bank has an important role to play through policy and regulatory reform, investing in enabling infrastructure and local processing capacity, project finance and de-risking, and strengthening natural resource management.  This includes deep-sea mining, where the Bank can play a catalytic role by providing knowledge and guidance in a nascent sector. Directing resources to countries most in need is not enough; the Bank must position those resources to deliver value.  Procurement policies that reward distortive industrial policies, encourage subsidies, and incentivize corruption and collusion ultimately undermine development, stifle the private sector, and result in higher long-term costs.  The Bank must pursue procurement reforms that result in greater competition and quality.  We recognize recent efforts to expand the use of quality-based procurement approaches, boost the use of local labor, and improve industry outreach, but much of this was necessary just to move closer to the value-for-money objective embodied in the Procurement Framework adopted over a decade ago.  The Bank needs to assess where its current procurement framework, policies, and implementation are still not delivering competition and quality needed for long-term development and adopt further reforms and capacity-building measures to address those shortcomings.  The Bank’s peer institutions are implementing a robust procurement reform agenda.  We expect the World Bank to lead on these efforts rather than fall behind. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) can play an important role in mobilizing private capital to support economic growth and private sector development.  But higher mobilization levels are not a substitute for the harder work of creating markets and crowding in truly private investment in poorer, less creditworthy countries.  We call on the IFC to redouble efforts to meet its 2018 capital increase pledge to make 40 percent of new commitments in the poorest and most fragile countries.  The IFC’s rate of progress towards this commitment has fallen unacceptably short, underscoring the need to align the institution more closely with its core mission. Finally, the IMF and World Bank are ultimately taxpayer-funded public institutions whose budgets should reflect the narrower set of operations that comes with refocusing on their core missions.  We appreciate the flat real administrative budget growth being pursued at both institutions this fiscal year, and expect to see this same approach in future years.  Both institutions and their Governors can and should go further, including by indefinitely freezing – and even reducing – Executive Board budgets and salaries, which now have a combined annual cost over $200 million.  The reduction in the IMF Board’s core budget this year is an important first step in this direction.  The Boards are significantly more expensive, both in overall and per-capita terms, than at other international financial institutions.  Every unnecessary dollar spent on the Boards is a dollar that cannot be used to reduce poverty, promote macroeconomic stability, or  foster growth.  The Bank, Fund, and their members must do more to restrain these inexcusably bloated budgets.  We also call on the IMF to divest from the Bretton Woods Recreation Center and the Concordia Hotel. Streamlining policy priorities will allow both the World Bank and IMF to focus limited public resources on effectively fulfilling their core mandates while responding to crises.  We look forward to working with Management, staff, and other shareholders, to accomplish this task. ###

title: Treasury and IRS Move to Protect Health Care Benefits for Eligible Americans
body: October 14, 2026 Proposed Rules Implement Working Families Tax Cuts Reforms to Prevent Fraud and Abuse of the Premium Tax Credit WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued proposed regulations to implement President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts reforms to the Premium Tax Credit (PTC), a refundable tax credit that helps eligible American taxpayers afford health insurance purchased through the Health Insurance Exchanges. “Hardworking American taxpayers should not be forced to subsidize health care for people who are ineligible under federal law,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent . “Today’s proposed rules implement the common-sense reforms enacted by the Working Families Tax Cuts to close eligibility loopholes and ensure taxpayer-funded Premium Tax Credits are reserved for eligible Americans. Under President Trump, this Administration is cracking down on fraud and corruption; holding bad actors accountable; lowering health care costs for Americans; and restoring integrity to our tax code and health care system.” “The proposed rules protect eligible taxpayers while strengthening the integrity of the Premium Tax Credit,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano . “The enhanced verification measures are designed to curb improper claims, ensuring these vital tax benefits go strictly to the hardworking Americans who qualify for them.” “The Trump Administration’s whole-of-government approach to fighting fraud, waste, and abuse is built on the idea that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz . “Ensuring health programs serve only those who are eligible is one of the most effective ways to protect these programs and the taxpayers who support them. With today’s proposed rules, the Treasury Department is taking another step forward in our collaborative effort to protect taxpayer dollars by shutting down waste and fraud before a single dollar leaves the building.” PROTECTING TAXPAYER-FUNDED BENEFITS FOR ELIGIBLE AMERICANS The proposed rules put the Working Families Tax Cuts’ Premium Tax Credit reforms into effect which strengthen eligibility checks, close gaps in the verification process, and help ensure taxpayer-funded subsidies go only to eligible American taxpayers. The Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud exposed the need for stronger safeguards to protect the integrity of the Federal Marketplace. As part of that work, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced the removal of more than 760,000 unverified “phantom” enrollees from the rolls of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), resulting in $2.2 billion in savings and sending nearly 1 million Americans $500 each who had been overcharged for their Obamacare coverage by the Biden Administration. The Treasury and IRS proposed rules: Strengthen Eligibility Standards: Beginning in 2027, ensures taxpayer-funded health insurance subsidies go only to Americans who qualify under federal law. Protect Taxpayer Benefits for Eligible Americans: Restricts PTC eligibility to U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and certain lawfully present noncitizens. Close Verification Gaps: Applies commonsense PTC eligibility checks and adds new verification criteria for any advance PTC payments. The proposed regulations are available here . The changes to Exchange procedures and operations necessary to implement the verification requirements are expected to be addressed in parallel proposed regulations issued by HHS under related provisions of the same statute. ###

title: October 14, 2026 - FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development Effort begins by Soliciting Public Feedback For Immediate Release: October 14, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), today announced the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to reimagine the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. As outlined in a new white paper , the Initiative will develop an optimized, fit-for-purpose framework that reflects the realities of rare disease drug development by considering the nuances of each disease, patient needs, product type and the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations. To solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative from patients and disease advocates, industry, and others, the FDA will host an October 28 meeting at the FDA’s White Oak campus. The meeting will be facilitated by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA. “Americans with rare diseases cannot afford a regulatory system that treats every condition the same,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump, FDA is rethinking rare disease drug development by putting patients at the center and matching regulatory requirements to the realities of small patient populations. We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.” “Patients and families living with rare diseases have few or no approved treatment options, and the burden of uncertainty can extend across every part of their lives,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront — prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them. The FDA will fight hard for patients by building a more consistent, predictable, and innovative approach to rare disease drug development while maintaining the rigorous standards Americans expect from the FDA.” The FDA has long used regulatory flexibility and developed targeted programs to support innovation in the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. These efforts have led to meaningful advances for patients and families. Nevertheless, with only 5% or so of rare conditions having an FDA-approved treatment, the FDA agrees with patients, drug developers, and providers that more must be done to speed the development of safe and effective treatments for rare diseases. In developing the framework, the FDA is committed to the following: Providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication. Embedding the patient’s voice both early, and at clearly defined milestones, in the drug development and review process. Further leveraging external expertise to support customization of regulatory review. Building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review. Applying risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections. Championing the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and innovative statistical approaches in rare disease drug development. The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards,” said the Hub’s Director, Amy Comstock Rick, J.D. “A bold vision to reimagine the framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.” Further opportunities to provide input will follow the public meeting, including sector-specific roundtables, Requests for Information, and internal FDA feedback sessions. This feedback will inform the detailed development of a new framework, which might include potential new or revised guidance, revisions to regulations, staff training, and organizational changes. Additional Resources • FDA Rare Disease Innovation Hub • Rare Disease Framework Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: October 14, 2026 - FDA Approves First Treatment for Certain People With BCG-Unresponsive Bladder Cancer
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Treatment for Certain People With BCG-Unresponsive Bladder Cancer Expanded approval of Anktiva marks a new FDA approach to using evidence across closely related forms of bladder cancer For Immediate Release: October 14, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today expanded the approved use of Anktiva (nogapendekin alfa inbakicept-pmln), given with Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), to include adults with high-grade papillary-only bladder cancer that has not spread into the bladder muscle and has not responded to BCG treatment. Anktiva is the first FDA-approved treatment specifically for patients with BCG-unresponsive, high-grade papillary-only disease. The approval marks a new FDA approach to evaluating treatments for BCG-unresponsive non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). The agency based its decision on evidence supporting an earlier approval of Anktiva for adults with another form of NMIBC, carcinoma in situ (CIS), with or without papillary tumors, and scientific similarities between CIS and high-grade papillary-only disease. “We listen to patients, clinicians, and researchers, and we act when the science supports a new approach,” said R. Angelo de Claro, M.D., Director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “For Anktiva, our review of the similarities between these cancers allowed us to build on the results in patients with CIS and expand treatment options for people with high-grade papillary tumors alone. This approach may also help guide the development of future treatments.” NMIBC is bladder cancer that has not grown into the bladder’s muscle layer and can include CIS and papillary tumors. CIS forms flat patches along the bladder’s lining, while papillary tumors grow from the lining into the bladder as small, finger-like projections. CIS is always high-grade, while papillary tumors can be low-grade or high-grade. High-grade cancers are more likely to grow and spread than low-grade cancers. Treatment for high-risk NMIBC often starts with BCG, which activates the immune system inside the bladder to fight cancer. Sometimes, however, the cancer persists or returns. Adding Anktiva gives the immune system another way to fight the cancer, and the combination can help some people whose cancer was not controlled by BCG alone. Anktiva’s CIS approval was supported by a trial ( NCT03022825 ) that evaluated the treatment’s effectiveness in 77 adults, some of whom also had papillary tumors. Sixty-two percent achieved a complete response, meaning no high-grade cancer was detected during follow-up assessments, and of those, 58% maintained that response for at least 12 months and 40% for at least 24 months. For today’s expanded approval, the FDA considered these results alongside clinical and laboratory evidence showing that CIS and high-grade papillary tumors share important features. They often occur together, can be difficult to distinguish under a microscope and carry a high risk of returning or progressing when BCG treatment no longer works. These similarities supported applying the evidence of Anktiva’s effectiveness in people with CIS to those with high-grade papillary-only disease. To help developers apply this approach, the FDA is working toward finalizing its draft guidance, “ Bacillus Calmette-Guérin-Unresponsive Nonmuscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: Developing Drugs and Biological Products for Treatment .” The guidance is intended to include discussion of using evidence from studies in patients with CIS to support approval of treatments for BCG-unresponsive, high-grade papillary-only NMIBC. Anktiva is given with BCG directly into the bladder through a catheter. It is given once a week for six weeks, with additional treatment based on how the cancer responds. Treatment may continue for up to 37 months. It should be stopped if the cancer persists after a second six-week course, returns or progresses, or side effects become unacceptable. The most common side effects and laboratory abnormalities included painful or frequent urination, an urgent need to urinate, blood in the urine, urinary tract infections, muscle or joint pain, chills, fever, and increased blood levels of creatinine and potassium. Anktiva’s prescribing information warns that delaying surgery to remove all or part of the bladder can allow the cancer to spread to other parts of the body, which can be fatal. The approval was granted to Altor BioScience, LLC. Additional Resources FDA Anktiva Approval Announcement Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: October 5, 2026 - FDA Seeks Public Input to Support Ibogaine Research
body: FDA News Release FDA Seeks Public Input to Support Ibogaine Research For Immediate Release: October 05, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced a request for information (RFI) describing approaches the agency is considering for the design of early-phase clinical trials of ibogaine drug products and seeking public input on those approaches. The RFI seeks comments, data, and information on specific protocol elements relevant to ibogaine drug development, including dose selection and escalation, care setting, safety monitoring, eligibility criteria, stopping rules and safety oversight. This RFI marks the latest FDA action to advance President Trump’s April 2026 executive order on Accelerating Medical Treatments for Serious Mental Illness , which directed agencies to accelerate research into psychedelic medicine. “Patients facing serious conditions that have not responded to existing treatments deserve rigorous scientific investigation of promising new approaches,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “With ibogaine, there are important scientific questions as well as serious safety concerns. We are seeking high-quality data and input that can help inform clinical research while putting patient safety first.” The FDA is seeking comments, data and information in four primary areas: General study design , including appropriate patient populations; Dose selection and escalation , including the proposed use of small, sequential dose-ascending groups and a starting dose justified by available data and not exceeding 10 mg/kg; Safety considerations , including monitoring for cardiac and neurologic adverse events and other safeguards for clinical trials; and Ethical and oversight considerations , including informed consent and appropriate independent safety oversight. The FDA recognizes the seriousness of the conditions and unmet needs that patients seeking ibogaine treatments face. The information received through this RFI may help the agency better understand the potential uses, benefits and risks of ibogaine drug products and inform approaches to drug development. The FDA has been working across the federal government to support the responsible development of ibogaine drug products through careful evidence-based processes. In July 2026, the FDA issued its finalized guidance for industry, Psychedelic Drugs: Considerations for Clinical Investigations , which provides general considerations for sponsors developing psychedelic drugs. The FDA has also allowed an early-phase clinical study of noribogaine hydrochloride , a derivative of ibogaine, to proceed under an Investigational New Drug application as a potential treatment for alcohol use disorder. As part of the whole-of-government approach to advance psychedelic drug development, HHS, through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) , is funding a program to collect safety and efficacy data through early-phase clinical trials, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) is funding research on ibogaine for the potential treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD). Based on available data and the seriousness of the conditions, HHS is prioritizing two initial populations for federally supported research: adults with OUD and adults with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The public will have 45 days following publication in the Federal Register to submit comments, data or information to the docket. Stakeholders are encouraged to submit comments electronically at regulations.gov by searching for Docket No. FDA-2026-N-10429 . Written/paper submissions may also be sent to: Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852. The comment period closes Friday, November 20, 2026. Late comments will not be considered. title: October 1, 2026 - FDA Approves First Heart Valve Designed to Grow with Children
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Heart Valve Designed to Grow with Children For Immediate Release: October 01, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve, a surgically implanted pulmonary heart valve for pediatric patients with congenital pulmonary valve disease. This innovative device may reduce the need for repeat open-heart surgeries in children with heart defects, reflecting the Trump Administration’s commitment to bringing breakthrough medical technologies to market as quickly and safely as possible. The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve is the first heart valve designed to be expanded after surgery to keep pace with a child’s growth, and the first valve approved in the U.S. to use polymeric material rather than animal-derived tissue for its inner flaps (called leaflets). “For far too long, children with congenital heart defects who need pulmonary valve replacement have had very limited surgical options, and those options have historically required multiple open-heart surgeries as children grow,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Today’s landmark approval is a historic turning point and reflects the Trump Administration and the FDA’s commitment to help bring innovative, life-changing devices to the patients who need them most.” Congenital heart defects are among the most common types of birth defects in the United States, affecting about 1 in every 100 births. Among these conditions are pulmonary valve abnormalities — including pulmonary valve stenosis, in which the valve is narrowed, and pulmonary valve atresia, in which the valve fails to form normally — both of which restrict blood flow from the heart to the lungs. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , pulmonary valve atresia and stenosis together affect around 4,200 babies in the United States each year. While treatment can improve blood flow and help repair these congenital defects, some children may be left with significant pulmonary regurgitation, or leakage of blood back through the pulmonary valve. Over time, this can weaken or enlarge the right ventricle and create a need for pulmonary valve replacement as the child grows. “For children born with congenital heart disease, valve replacement timing has always been a difficult decision — wait too long and you risk harm to the child, but intervene too early and they may need multiple open-heart surgeries as they grow,” said Michelle Tarver, M.D., Ph.D., director of the FDA’s Center for Devices and Radiological Health . “The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve gives doctors the option of far fewer trips to the operating room, which may result in better quality of life for these children and their families.” The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve can be initially implanted as small as approximately 13 millimeters in diameter — the right size for a toddler or preschool-aged child — and later widened using a small inflatable tube (balloon catheter) as the child grows, eventually reaching up to 22 millimeters, which is comparable to an adult-sized pulmonary valve. In addition, the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve uses polymeric material for its leaflets — the flaps inside the valve that open and close to control blood flow. Traditional valves use tissue derived from animals, which tends to harden and break down faster in children, often requiring earlier repeat surgery. One-year follow-up data suggest the Autus valve’s synthetic leaflets hold up well over time. This is the first time the FDA has approved a valve that uses polymeric leaflet material for any indication. The FDA’s approval is based on data from a clinical study, which enrolled 62 pediatric patients across 12 U.S. sites. At the six-month follow-up, the first 60 patients demonstrated acceptable hemodynamic performance, meaning blood flow through the right side of the heart was within acceptable limits, and there was no more than mild leakage back through the valve. All patients in the study had a successful procedure, with no deaths, blood clots requiring additional treatment, strokes or other clot-related complications. Three patients experienced a fracture in the valve frame and two patients had reduced movement of one of the valve leaflets (the flaps that open and close), but none of these events resulted in symptoms for the patients. Additionally, valve performance began deteriorating in two patients who started to outgrow it. Both patients had their valves successfully expanded without an invasive surgical procedure, but the experience is limited. Longer-term studies are being conducted to better understand these risks, and to collect more data to show that expansion can maintain a functional valve that may lead to fewer surgical procedures for patients. The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve is the first pediatric approval to come out of the FDA’s Total Product Life Cycle Advisory Program (TAP) , a voluntary program for device developers intended to spur more rapid development of high-quality, safe, effective and innovative medical devices for all patients. The FDA previously granted the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve Breakthrough Device designation , which is meant to expedite the development and review of devices that provide for more effective treatment or diagnosis of life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating diseases or conditions. The Autus Size-Adjustable Valve was approved through the premarket approval pathway, the FDA’s most stringent type of medical device marketing application. The pathway is used for certain Class III devices, which generally pose the greatest risk. Before approving a device, the FDA reviews scientific evidence, including nonclinical and clinical data, to determine whether there is reasonable assurance that the device is safe and effective for its intended use and whether the benefits outweigh the known risks. Edwards Lifesciences received approval for the Autus Size-Adjustable Valve, developed by Autus Valve Technologies Inc. title: September 30, 2026 - FDA Launches Nationwide Effort to Expand Scientific Expertise and Consumer Voices to Advisory Committees
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches Nationwide Effort to Expand Scientific Expertise and Consumer Voices to Advisory Committees For Immediate Release: September 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced a broad, nationwide recruitment effort to expand the range of qualified voices and perspectives on its advisory committees— the independent bodies that inform some of the most consequential decisions in American public health. As part of an effort to broaden and strengthen participation on its advisory committees, the FDA is publishing two Federal Register notices: one seeking qualified scientific, technical, and professional voting members across all committees with current or anticipated vacancies, and a companion notice seeking consumer representatives to ensure the public’s voice is at the table. “FDA advisory committees bring together leading scientific minds to engage with the most difficult questions in public health. We are actively inviting people from across the country who are on the forefront of their fields — clinicians, researchers, and community voices who can bring the latest science, real-world experience, and fresh perspectives to the FDA’s deliberations,” said Acting FDA Commissioner of Food and Drugs, Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “These panels provide independent expertise and rigorous scrutiny as the FDA navigates complex and rapidly evolving areas of science. The Trump Administration is deeply committed to strengthening the partnership between the FDA and the nation’s brightest minds. Advisory committees are a cornerstone of the FDA’s science-based, transparent regulatory process. These committees and panels bring together scientific experts such as physicians, researchers, biostatisticians, along with patient advocates and consumer representatives to evaluate the evidence on drugs, vaccines, biologics, medical devices, and other FDA-regulated products — providing independent recommendations that help the FDA make well-informed decisions on behalf of the American public. The FDA is recruiting qualified candidates for vacancies spanning multiple scientific domains — from oncology and cardiovascular medicine to neurology, genetics, and medical devices. Interested candidates — whether applying as scientific experts or as consumer representatives — are encouraged to begin the process through the centralized FDA Advisory Committee Membership Nomination application portal . Nominees for scientific and technical voting member positions must demonstrate subject-matter expertise relevant to one or more FDA advisory committees, the ability to interpret complex scientific and technical information, an understanding of the public health significance of issues before the committee, and the capacity to provide objective, independent advice. Nominees for consumer representative positions should have demonstrated affiliation with or active participation in consumer or community-based organizations, and the ability to analyze technical data, discuss benefits and risks, and evaluate product safety and efficacy from a public perspective. The FDA will consider nominations for current and anticipated near-term vacancies and will accept nominations on a continuing basis. To receive first consideration for current and near-term vacancies, nominations for consumer representative positions should be submitted no later than November 15, 2026, and nominations for scientific, technical, professional, and other voting-member positions should be submitted no later than November 30, 2026. Nominations received after these dates will be considered as later vacancies arise. Self-nominations are accepted. Members are invited to serve for terms of up to four years.
